Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto is a Japanese kami worshipped at [[Aso Shrine]]. He is a grandson of Jimmu.<ref name="Ponsonby">Ponsonby-Fane, ''Shrines,'' pp. 480-484.</ref>
He is the son of [[Kamuyaimimi]]<ref name="Takano-2006" />, and grandson of [[Jimmu]].<ref name="Ponsonby" />
[[ja:健磐龍命]]
== Chief Priest == The position of Chief Priest of Aso Shrine is hereditary and is passed down from generation to generation with the oldest male in the family becoming the new head of the shrine. The Aso family has the second oldest recorded lineage in Japan after the Imperial family. The family themselves are said to be descendants of Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. The Aso family were priests but also rose to power as a powerful samurai clan in the 11th century. They remained in prominence until the 16th century as their feudal lord continued to rule over half of what is now known as Kumamoto Prefecture. This contributed economically to the family and the shrine, allowing them to rebuild shrine buildings and hold festivals. It also made it possible for them to establish branches of the Aso shrine in other locations. Some of those shrines still remain in up to 500 locations to this day. Koreyuki Aso (''Aso Koreyuki in Japanese name order'') was the 91st Chief Priest of Aso Shrine with his son being the 92nd.<ref name="Takano-2006">{{Cite book|title=History and Festivals of the Aso Shrine|last1=Takano|first1=Tomoaki|last2=Uchimura|first2=Hiroaki|publisher=Aso Shrine|year=2006|location=Aso Shrine, Ichinomiya, Aso City.}}</ref>

{{short description|Shinto shrine in Kumamoto Prefecture, Japan}}\ {{nihongo|'''Aso Shrine'''|阿蘇神社|''Aso-jinja''}} is a [[Jinja (shrine)|Shinto Shrine]] in [[Aso, Kumamoto|Aso]], [[Kumamoto Prefecture]], [[Japan]].<ref name="studies477">[[Richard Ponsonby-Fane|Ponsonby-Fane, Richard]]. (1962). ''Studies in Shinto and Shrines,'' p. 477; Kotodamaya.com, [http://www.kotodamaya.com/aso-jinja/ "Aso Jinja"]; retrieved 2012-10-29.</ref> Aso is one of the oldest [[shrine]]s in Japan.<ref name="jnto1">{{cite web|website=[[Japan National Tourist Organization|JNTO]] |url=http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/attractions/facilities/spots/shrines_temples/83dn3a000000ek1x.html|title=Aso-jinja Shrine|url-status=dead|archive-date=2017-10-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171015222732/http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/attractions/facilities/spots/shrines_temples/83dn3a000000ek1x.html}}</ref> This shrine holds several [[Important Cultural Properties of Japan|Important Cultural Properties]], including ''Ichi-no-shinden'' (一の神殿), ''Ni-no-shinden'' (二の神殿), and ''Rōmon'' (楼門). The Aso family in charge of the shrine is said to have the second oldest recorded lineage in Japan after the [[Imperial House of Japan|Imperial]] family. The Aso Shrine was heavily damaged in the [[2016 Kumamoto earthquakes]]. The shrine's ''[[rōmon]]'' (tower gate) completely collapsed. The ''[[Haiden (Shinto)|haiden]]'' (worshiping hall) also collapsed.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20160416/p2a/00m/0na/023000c|title=Designated national cultural asset at Aso Shrine collapses in Kumamoto quake|publisher=Mainichi Shimbun|date=2016-04-16|access-date=2016-04-16}}</ref>[[File:Tennō Jimmu.jpg|thumb|248x248px|Emperor Jimmu, who is said to be an ancestor of Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto.]]

=== U-no-matsuri === The Aso shrine's ''U-no-matsuri'' (卯の祭) is a 13-day event that occurs in March to welcome spring and pray for the beginning of the rice planting season. The U-no-matsuri marks the anniversary of Aso shrine's chief deity ''Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto's'' arrival in Aso. This event occurred in the second month of the lunar calendar which is March in the current calendar. The shrine's Guuji San perform sacred Shinto music and dances every day of the festival while praying for a rich harvest.<ref name="Takano-2006" />
Occurring simultaneously to the U-no-matsuri, is a prominent festival called the ''Tazukuri Matsuri'' (田作り祭り) which is celebrated over 7 days, and the ''Daihimonjiyaki'' (大火文字焼き) which is the lighting of the Chinese characters for "fire" and "flame" on the mountains which is also done around the same time and sometimes the same day as the Tazukuri Matsuri.<ref name="末吉-2018">{{Cite book|title=肥後一の宮阿蘇神社|last=末吉|first=駿一|publisher=(株）マインド|year=2018|pages=38, 39, 40 and 43}}</ref>
== Burial ground == Behind the haiden in Aso shrine are the three smaller shrines said to house Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto and the other 11 kami of Aso shrine. [[en:Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto]] {{draft}} {{Infobox noble|reign-type=[[神武天皇]]の[[皇子]]|birth_date=unknown|father=[[Kamuyaimimi]]|name=Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto|spouse=Asotsuhime no Mikoto|issue=Hayamikatama no Mikoto}}
Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto is a Japanese kami worshipped at [[Aso Shrine]]. He is a grandson of Jimmu.<ref name="Ponsonby">Ponsonby-Fane, ''Shrines,'' pp. 480-484.</ref>
He is the son of [[Kamuyaimimi]]<ref name="Takano-2006" />, and grandson of [[Jimmu]].<ref name="Ponsonby" />
[[ja:健磐龍命]]
== Chief Priest == The position of Chief Priest of Aso Shrine is hereditary and is passed down from generation to generation with the oldest male in the family becoming the new head of the shrine. The Aso family has the second oldest recorded lineage in Japan after the Imperial family. The family themselves are said to be descendants of Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. The Aso family were priests but also rose to power as a powerful samurai clan in the 11th century. They remained in prominence until the 16th century as their feudal lord continued to rule over half of what is now known as Kumamoto Prefecture. This contributed economically to the family and the shrine, allowing them to rebuild shrine buildings and hold festivals. It also made it possible for them to establish branches of the Aso shrine in other locations. Some of those shrines still remain in up to 500 locations to this day. Koreyuki Aso (''Aso Koreyuki in Japanese name order'') was the 91st Chief Priest of Aso Shrine with his son being the 92nd.<ref name="Takano-2006">{{Cite book|title=History and Festivals of the Aso Shrine|last1=Takano|first1=Tomoaki|last2=Uchimura|first2=Hiroaki|publisher=Aso Shrine|year=2006|location=Aso Shrine, Ichinomiya, Aso City.}}</ref>

== Mythological background == He is the son of [[Kamuyaimimi]]<ref name="Takano-2006" />, and grandson of [[Jimmu]].<ref name="Ponsonby" />
The shrine is dedicated to the veneration of [[Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto]] (健磐龍命), who was a grandson of Japan's first emperor and the nephew of [[Emperor Suizei]], the second monarch on the traditional list of emperors.<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' p. 29.</ref> In the same period that [[Emperor Jimmu]] was establishing his palace at [[Kashihara]] at the foot of [[Yamato Sanzan|Mount Unebi]] in [[Yamato Province|Yamato province]],<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, ''Imperial House,'' p. 28; [http://www.kunaicho.go.jp/ryobo/guide/001/index.html ''Unebiyama-no Ushitora-no-sumi-no misasagi'' (''Unebi Goryō,'' tomb of Emperor Jimmu).]</ref> Takeiwatasu was sent to Aso where he helped establish a number of agricultural communities; and later, he is said to have built a palace at [[Miyagi Prefecture|Miyagi]].<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, ''Shrines,'' pp. 480-484.</ref>
=== The creation of Aso === [[File:Ojodake.jpg|thumb|Ojodake on Mt. Aso where ''Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto'' practised his archery.]] According to an interview with several priests at Aso shrine, the legend of Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto and the formation of Aso City, is as follows:
Thousands of years ago, the crater now known as Aso city was said to be filled with water and was thereby a huge lake surrounded by the outer rim of the caldera. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto kicked in the western side of the caldera<ref name="Takano-2006" /> at what is now known as [[Tateno Station (Kumamoto)|Tateno]], [[Minamiaso, Kumamoto|Minami-Aso]]. He fell from the effort and was unable to stand for a while hence the name "Tateno" meaning "''unable to stand up''."As the water drained away forming rivers on the outside of the valley, a huge catfish (''[[Namazu (Japanese mythology)|Namazu]])'' appeared. The catfish was settled at the bottom of the lake where some stories say it was asked to leave by Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. The catfish went to Namazu, [[Kashima, Kumamoto|Kashima]] where Namazu-sha Shrine was established to pay homage to the soul of the catfish as the spirit of the lake. Now the shrine is in the precincts of the Kokuzo Shrine.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014">{{Cite news|url=http://www.aso-geopark.jp/|title=The Deity of the Volcano Geosite|date=2014|work=Aso GeoPark Geosite Map|publisher=Aso Local Development Design Centre Foundation|type=Guide Map}}</ref> [[File:Matoishi.jpg|thumb|The ''Matoishi'' (target stone) that Kihachi was sent to, to retrieve the arrows for Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto.]]
=== The legend of Kihachi === The legend of Kihachi surrounds the Hitaki-Shinji festival commemorated in Aso annually. Legend states that Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto liked practicing his archery. He would stand on Ojodake (a cone shaped formation on Mt. Aso) and practice shooting ''matoishi'' (target stone) in what is now Matoishi in Aso, located north of the caldera. Kihachi his servant, was in charge of bringing the arrows back from the ''matoishi'' to Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. After the 100th arrow was shot, Kihachi got tired and kicked the arrow back breaking it in half. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto was furious and drawing his sword slayed Kihachi cutting off his head. Kihachi's head ascended as a deity vowing to exact revenge on Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto's village of Aso. Later, during the winter months it frosted in Aso valley damaging all of the crops. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto realised that this was the revenge that Kihachi had spoken of and so he enshrined his soul at ''Shimo Shrine'' (''frost shrine'') to abate his anger. A ritual called the Hitaki-Shinji was started where a fire is kept for 2 months to pray for a good harvest and prevent frost damage to the crops.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014" /> They say that this is why the winters in Aso are so cold.
== Burial ground == Behind the haiden in Aso shrine are the three smaller shrines said to house Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto and the other 11 kami of Aso shrine. These are the ''ichi-no-shinden'' built in 天保11年 (1840), the ''ni-no-shinden'' built in 天保 13 年(1842), and the ''san-no-shinden'' built in 天保 14年 (1843).<ref name="Honda-2019">{{Cite book|title=阿蘇神社|last=Honda|first=Fujio|publisher=Gakken Publishing Company|year=2019|language=ja}}</ref>
==Worship== Aso-no-Ōkami, the ''[[kami]]'' or spirit who is believed to dwell at Aso Shrine has been worshipped from early times{{vague|date=November 2014}} as the guardian deity of safety in navigation, and today, Aso-no-Ōkami is seen as protecting worshippers from traffic accidents and other untoward events.<ref name="jnto1">{{cite web|title=Aso-jinja Shrine|url=http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/attractions/facilities/spots/shrines_temples/83dn3a000000ek1x.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171015222732/http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/attractions/facilities/spots/shrines_temples/83dn3a000000ek1x.html|archive-date=2017-10-15|website=[[Japan National Tourist Organization|JNTO]]}}</ref>
[[Yabusame]] is an annual festival which brings together horse-mounted archers, special arrows and targets, and Shinto ritual at Aso Shrine.<ref>[http://edpas.net/journal/109/ Yabusame at Aso Shrine] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081204191951/http://edpas.net/journal/109/|date=December 4, 2008}}</ref>
The ''Aso no Himatsuri'' festival has its origin in the month of March festivals such as ''Aso no Noyaki'' (the first burning in Aso) and ''Aso jinja no Hifuri shinji'' (the fire ritual of Aso Shrine).<ref>[http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/ JAL Guide to Japan:] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061026103601/http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/|date=2006-10-26}} [http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/city_information/fuk/ Fukuoaka]; {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061026165358/http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/city_information/fuk/|date=2006-10-26}} JNTO: [http://www.iexplore.com/dmap/Japan/Event/16312 Fire Festivals.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607060650/http://www.iexplore.com/dmap/Japan/Event/16312|date=June 7, 2011}}</ref> Although rarely performed today, ceremonies which honor ancestors who settled near the [[Aso Caldera|Aso caldera]] do continue to be associated with the Aso jinja.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Akimoto|first1=Kazuhide|last2=Nakamura|first2=Minako|date=November 15, 2008|title=Settlement Composition and Actual Condition of Grave Festivals in Aso Caldera Settlements|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.3130/jaabe.7.209|journal=Journal of Asian Architecture and Building Engineering|volume=7|issue=2|pages=209-216|doi=10.3130/jaabe.7.209|doi-access=free}}</ref>
=== Deities === [[File:Origin_of_Iwato_Kagura_Dance_Amaterasu_by_Toyokuni_III_(Kunisada)_1856.png|thumb|The Goddess ''Amaterasu'' is said to be the source of ''Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto's'' divine powers, as her descendant.|259x259px]] The shrine's main kami is ''Ichinomiya Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto'' (一の宮健磐龍命) the creator of [[Aso, Kumamoto|Aso]] and the God credited with teaching the villagers about agriculture. He is said to be the descendant of Emperor Jinmu. Since Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto was descended from Emperor Jinmu who is said to have been human, legends surrounding his divinity is unclear. Some state that through his lineage from the Goddess [[Amaterasu]] he was given divine powers for creating Aso. Another legend states that the deity of the volcano, entered the body of Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto turning him from a human into a divine being. These are common folklore among the people with the only consensus being that over time, the deity of the land and the deity of the volcano was combined into one symbol by the name of ''Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto''.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014" />
The second important deity is called ''Ninomiya Aso-tsu-hime-no-mikoto'' the wife of ''Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto'' (二の宮阿蘇都媛命).
The third important deity mentioned is ''Juuichinomiya Kuni-no-miyatsuko-hayamikatama-no-mikoto'' (十一の宮園造速瓶玉命).
The other deities are the kami of fire 火の神, the kami of water 水の神 flowing near the ''rōmon'' gate of the shrine and the other kami of agriculture 農の神.
=== U-no-matsuri === The Aso shrine's ''U-no-matsuri'' (卯の祭) is a 13-day event that occurs in March to welcome spring and pray for the beginning of the rice planting season. This event occurred in the second month of the lunar calendar which is March in the current calendar. The shrine's Guuji San perform sacred Shinto music and dances every day of the festival while praying for a rich harvest.<ref name="Takano-2006" />
Occurring simultaneously to the U-no-matsuri, is a prominent festival called the ''Tazukuri Matsuri'' (田作り祭り) which is celebrated over 7 days, and the ''Daihimonjiyaki'' (大火文字焼き) which is the lighting of the Chinese characters for "fire" and "flame" on the mountains which is also done around the same time and sometimes the same day as the Tazukuri Matsuri.<ref name="末吉-2018">{{Cite book|title=肥後一の宮阿蘇神社|last=末吉|first=駿一|publisher=(株）マインド|year=2018|pages=38, 39, 40 and 43}}</ref>

Kihachi his servant, was in charge of bringing the arrows back from the ''matoishi'' to Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. After the 100th arrow was shot, Kihachi got tired and kicked the arrow back breaking it in half. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto was furious and drawing his sword slayed Kihachi cutting off his head. Kihachi's head ascended as a deity vowing to exact revenge on Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto's village of Aso. Later, during the winter months it frosted in Aso valley damaging all of the crops. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto realised that this was the revenge that Kihachi had spoken of and so he enshrined his soul at ''Shimo Shrine'' (''frost shrine'') to abate his anger. A ritual called the Hitaki-Shinji was started where a fire is kept for 2 months to pray for a good harvest and prevent frost damage to the crops.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014" /> They say that this is why the winters in Aso are so cold.
=== Hereditary succession === The position of Chief Priest of Aso Shrine is hereditary and is passed down from generation to generation with the oldest male in the family becoming the new head of the shrine. The Aso family has the second oldest recorded lineage in Japan after the Imperial family. The family themselves are said to be descendants of Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. The Aso family were priests but also rose to power as a powerful samurai clan in the 11th century. They remained in prominence until the 16th century as their feudal lord continued to rule over half of what is now known as Kumamoto Prefecture. This contributed economically to the family and the shrine, allowing them to rebuild shrine buildings and hold festivals. It also made it possible for them to establish branches of the Aso shrine in other locations. Some of those shrines still remain in up to 500 locations to this day. Koreyuki Aso (''Aso Koreyuki in Japanese name order'') was the 91st Chief Priest of Aso Shrine with his son being the 92nd.<ref name="Takano-2006">{{Cite book|title=History and Festivals of the Aso Shrine|last1=Takano|first1=Tomoaki|last2=Uchimura|first2=Hiroaki|publisher=Aso Shrine|year=2006|location=Aso Shrine, Ichinomiya, Aso City.}}</ref>

[[File:Tennō Jimmu.jpg|thumb|248x248px|Emperor Jimmu, who is said to be an ancestor of Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto.]] ==Worship== Aso-no-Ōkami, the ''[[kami]]'' or spirit who is believed to dwell at Aso Shrine has been worshipped from early times{{vague|date=November 2014}} as the guardian deity of safety in navigation, and today, Aso-no-Ōkami is seen as protecting worshippers from traffic accidents and other untoward events.<ref name="jnto1">{{cite web|title=Aso-jinja Shrine|url=http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/attractions/facilities/spots/shrines_temples/83dn3a000000ek1x.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171015222732/http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/attractions/facilities/spots/shrines_temples/83dn3a000000ek1x.html|archive-date=2017-10-15|website=[[Japan National Tourist Organization|JNTO]]}}</ref>
[[Yabusame]] is an annual festival which brings together horse-mounted archers, special arrows and targets, and Shinto ritual at Aso Shrine.<ref>[http://edpas.net/journal/109/ Yabusame at Aso Shrine] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081204191951/http://edpas.net/journal/109/|date=December 4, 2008}}</ref>
The ''Aso no Himatsuri'' festival has its origin in the month of March festivals such as ''Aso no Noyaki'' (the first burning in Aso) and ''Aso jinja no Hifuri shinji'' (the fire ritual of Aso Shrine).<ref>[http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/ JAL Guide to Japan:] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061026103601/http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/|date=2006-10-26}} [http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/city_information/fuk/ Fukuoaka]; {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061026165358/http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/city_information/fuk/|date=2006-10-26}} JNTO: [http://www.iexplore.com/dmap/Japan/Event/16312 Fire Festivals.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607060650/http://www.iexplore.com/dmap/Japan/Event/16312|date=June 7, 2011}}</ref> Although rarely performed today, ceremonies which honor ancestors who settled near the [[Aso Caldera|Aso caldera]] do continue to be associated with the Aso jinja.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Akimoto|first1=Kazuhide|last2=Nakamura|first2=Minako|date=November 15, 2008|title=Settlement Composition and Actual Condition of Grave Festivals in Aso Caldera Settlements|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.3130/jaabe.7.209|journal=Journal of Asian Architecture and Building Engineering|volume=7|issue=2|pages=209-216|doi=10.3130/jaabe.7.209|doi-access=free}}</ref>
=== Deities === [[File:Origin_of_Iwato_Kagura_Dance_Amaterasu_by_Toyokuni_III_(Kunisada)_1856.png|thumb|The Goddess ''Amaterasu'' is said to be the source of ''Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto's'' divine powers, as her descendant.|259x259px]] The shrine's main kami is ''Ichinomiya Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto'' (一の宮健磐龍命) the creator of [[Aso, Kumamoto|Aso]] and the God credited with teaching the villagers about agriculture. He is said to be the descendant of Emperor Jinmu. Since Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto was descended from Emperor Jinmu who is said to have been human, legends surrounding his divinity is unclear. Some state that through his lineage from the Goddess [[Amaterasu]] he was given divine powers for creating Aso. Another legend states that the deity of the volcano, entered the body of Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto turning him from a human into a divine being. These are common folklore among the people with the only consensus being that over time, the deity of the land and the deity of the volcano was combined into one symbol by the name of ''Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto''.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014" />
The second important deity is called ''Ninomiya Aso-tsu-hime-no-mikoto'' the wife of ''Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto'' (二の宮阿蘇都媛命).
The third important deity mentioned is ''Juuichinomiya Kuni-no-miyatsuko-hayamikatama-no-mikoto'' (十一の宮園造速瓶玉命).
The other deities are the kami of fire 火の神, the kami of water 水の神 flowing near the ''rōmon'' gate of the shrine and the other kami of agriculture 農の神.
=== U-no-matsuri === The Aso shrine's ''U-no-matsuri'' (卯の祭) is a 13-day event that occurs in March to welcome spring and pray for the beginning of the rice planting season. The U-no-matsuri marks the anniversary of Aso shrine's chief deity ''Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto's'' arrival in Aso. This event occurred in the second month of the lunar calendar which is March in the current calendar. The shrine's Guuji San perform sacred Shinto music and dances every day of the festival while praying for a rich harvest.<ref name="Takano-2006" />
Occurring simultaneously to the U-no-matsuri, is a prominent festival called the ''Tazukuri Matsuri'' (田作り祭り) which is celebrated over 7 days, and the ''Daihimonjiyaki'' (大火文字焼き) which is the lighting of the Chinese characters for "fire" and "flame" on the mountains which is also done around the same time and sometimes the same day as the Tazukuri Matsuri.<ref name="末吉-2018">{{Cite book|title=肥後一の宮阿蘇神社|last=末吉|first=駿一|publisher=(株）マインド|year=2018|pages=38, 39, 40 and 43}}</ref>

[[en:Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto]] {{draft}} {{Infobox noble|reign-type=[[神武天皇]]の[[皇子]]|birth_date=unknown|father=[[Kamuyaimimi]]|name=Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto|spouse=Asotsuhime no Mikoto|issue=Hayamikatama no Mikoto}}
Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto is a Japanese kami worshipped at [[Aso Shrine]]. He is a grandson of Jimmu.<ref name="Ponsonby">Ponsonby-Fane, ''Shrines,'' pp. 480-484.</ref>
He is the son of [[Kamuyaimimi]]<ref name="Takano-2006" />, and grandson of [[Jimmu]].<ref name="Ponsonby" />
[[ja:健磐龍命]]
He is the {{ill|Oyagami|en}} of the {{ill|Aso clan|en}}.<ref name="Takano-2006" />
== Mythological background == He is the son of [[Kamuyaimimi]]<ref name="Takano-2006" />, and grandson of [[Jimmu]].<ref name="Ponsonby" />
The shrine is dedicated to the veneration of [[Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto]] (健磐龍命), who was a grandson of Japan's first emperor and the nephew of [[Emperor Suizei]], the second monarch on the traditional list of emperors.<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' p. 29.</ref> In the same period that [[Emperor Jimmu]] was establishing his palace at [[Kashihara]] at the foot of [[Yamato Sanzan|Mount Unebi]] in [[Yamato Province|Yamato province]],<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, ''Imperial House,'' p. 28; [http://www.kunaicho.go.jp/ryobo/guide/001/index.html ''Unebiyama-no Ushitora-no-sumi-no misasagi'' (''Unebi Goryō,'' tomb of Emperor Jimmu).]</ref> Takeiwatasu was sent to Aso where he helped establish a number of agricultural communities; and later, he is said to have built a palace at [[Miyagi Prefecture|Miyagi]].<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, ''Shrines,'' pp. 480-484.</ref>
=== The creation of Aso === [[File:Ojodake.jpg|thumb|Ojodake on Mt. Aso where ''Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto'' practised his archery.]] According to an interview with several priests at Aso shrine, the legend of Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto and the formation of Aso City, is as follows:
Thousands of years ago, the crater now known as Aso city was said to be filled with water and was thereby a huge lake surrounded by the outer rim of the caldera. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto kicked in the western side of the caldera<ref name="Takano-2006" /> at what is now known as [[Tateno Station (Kumamoto)|Tateno]], [[Minamiaso, Kumamoto|Minami-Aso]]. He fell from the effort and was unable to stand for a while hence the name "Tateno" meaning "''unable to stand up''."As the water drained away forming rivers on the outside of the valley, a huge catfish (''[[Namazu (Japanese mythology)|Namazu]])'' appeared. The catfish was settled at the bottom of the lake where some stories say it was asked to leave by Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. The catfish went to Namazu, [[Kashima, Kumamoto|Kashima]] where Namazu-sha Shrine was established to pay homage to the soul of the catfish as the spirit of the lake. Now the shrine is in the precincts of the Kokuzo Shrine.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014">{{Cite news|date=2014|title=The Deity of the Volcano Geosite|work=Aso GeoPark Geosite Map|publisher=Aso Local Development Design Centre Foundation|type=Guide Map|url=http://www.aso-geopark.jp/}}</ref> [[File:Matoishi.jpg|thumb|The ''Matoishi'' (target stone) that Kihachi was sent to, to retrieve the arrows for Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto.]]

[[en:Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto]] {{draft}} {{Infobox noble|reign-type=[[神武天皇]]の[[皇子]]|birth_date=unknown|father=[[Kamuyaimimi]]|name=Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto|spouse=Asotsuhime no Mikoto|issue=Hayamikatama no Mikoto}}
Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto is a Japanese kami worshipped at [[Aso Shrine]]. He is a grandson of Jimmu.<ref name="Ponsonby">Ponsonby-Fane, ''Shrines,'' pp. 480-484.</ref>
He is the son of [[Kamuyaimimi]]<ref name="Takano-2006" />, and grandson of [[Jimmu]].<ref name="Ponsonby" />
[[ja:健磐龍命]]
He is the {{ill|Oyagami|en}} of the {{ill|Aso clan|en|Aso clan}}.<ref name="Takano-2006" />
== Mythological background == He is the son of [[Kamuyaimimi]]<ref name="Takano-2006" />, and grandson of [[Jimmu]].<ref name="Ponsonby" />
The shrine is dedicated to the veneration of [[Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto]] (健磐龍命), who was a grandson of Japan's first emperor and the nephew of [[Emperor Suizei]], the second monarch on the traditional list of emperors.<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' p. 29.</ref> In the same period that [[Emperor Jimmu]] was establishing his palace at [[Kashihara]] at the foot of [[Yamato Sanzan|Mount Unebi]] in [[Yamato Province|Yamato province]],<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, ''Imperial House,'' p. 28; [http://www.kunaicho.go.jp/ryobo/guide/001/index.html ''Unebiyama-no Ushitora-no-sumi-no misasagi'' (''Unebi Goryō,'' tomb of Emperor Jimmu).]</ref> Takeiwatasu was sent to Aso where he helped establish a number of agricultural communities; and later, he is said to have built a palace at [[Miyagi Prefecture|Miyagi]].<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, ''Shrines,'' pp. 480-484.</ref>
=== The creation of Aso === [[File:Ojodake.jpg|thumb|Ojodake on Mt. Aso where ''Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto'' practised his archery.]] According to an interview with several priests at Aso shrine, the legend of Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto and the formation of Aso City, is as follows:
Thousands of years ago, the crater now known as Aso city was said to be filled with water and was thereby a huge lake surrounded by the outer rim of the caldera. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto kicked in the western side of the caldera<ref name="Takano-2006" /> at what is now known as [[Tateno Station (Kumamoto)|Tateno]], [[Minamiaso, Kumamoto|Minami-Aso]]. He fell from the effort and was unable to stand for a while hence the name "Tateno" meaning "''unable to stand up''."As the water drained away forming rivers on the outside of the valley, a huge catfish (''[[Namazu (Japanese mythology)|Namazu]])'' appeared. The catfish was settled at the bottom of the lake where some stories say it was asked to leave by Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. The catfish went to Namazu, [[Kashima, Kumamoto|Kashima]] where Namazu-sha Shrine was established to pay homage to the soul of the catfish as the spirit of the lake. Now the shrine is in the precincts of the Kokuzo Shrine.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014">{{Cite news|date=2014|title=The Deity of the Volcano Geosite|work=Aso GeoPark Geosite Map|publisher=Aso Local Development Design Centre Foundation|type=Guide Map|url=http://www.aso-geopark.jp/}}</ref> [[File:Matoishi.jpg|thumb|The ''Matoishi'' (target stone) that Kihachi was sent to, to retrieve the arrows for Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto.]]
=== The legend of Kihachi === The legend of Kihachi surrounds the Hitaki-Shinji festival commemorated in Aso annually. Legend states that Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto liked practicing his archery. He would stand on Ojodake (a cone shaped formation on Mt. Aso) and practice shooting ''matoishi'' (target stone) in what is now Matoishi in Aso, located north of the caldera. Kihachi his servant, was in charge of bringing the arrows back from the ''matoishi'' to Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. After the 100th arrow was shot, Kihachi got tired and kicked the arrow back breaking it in half. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto was furious and drawing his sword slayed Kihachi cutting off his head. Kihachi's head ascended as a deity vowing to exact revenge on Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto's village of Aso. Later, during the winter months it frosted in Aso valley damaging all of the crops. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto realised that this was the revenge that Kihachi had spoken of and so he enshrined his soul at ''Shimo Shrine'' (''frost shrine'') to abate his anger. A ritual called the Hitaki-Shinji was started where a fire is kept for 2 months to pray for a good harvest and prevent frost damage to the crops.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014" /> They say that this is why the winters in Aso are so cold.
=== Hereditary succession === The position of Chief Priest of Aso Shrine is hereditary and is passed down from generation to generation with the oldest male in the family becoming the new head of the shrine. The Aso family has the second oldest recorded lineage in Japan after the Imperial family. The family themselves are said to be descendants of Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. The Aso family were priests but also rose to power as a powerful samurai clan in the 11th century. They remained in prominence until the 16th century as their feudal lord continued to rule over half of what is now known as Kumamoto Prefecture. This contributed economically to the family and the shrine, allowing them to rebuild shrine buildings and hold festivals. It also made it possible for them to establish branches of the Aso shrine in other locations. Some of those shrines still remain in up to 500 locations to this day. Koreyuki Aso (''Aso Koreyuki in Japanese name order'') was the 91st Chief Priest of Aso Shrine with his son being the 92nd.<ref name="Takano-2006">{{Cite book|title=History and Festivals of the Aso Shrine|last1=Takano|first1=Tomoaki|last2=Uchimura|first2=Hiroaki|publisher=Aso Shrine|year=2006|location=Aso Shrine, Ichinomiya, Aso City.}}</ref>

[[File:Tennō Jimmu.jpg|thumb|248x248px|Emperor Jimmu, who is said to be an ancestor of Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto.]] ==Worship== Aso-no-Ōkami, the ''[[kami]]'' or spirit who is believed to dwell at Aso Shrine has been worshipped from early times{{vague|date=November 2014}} as the guardian deity of safety in navigation, and today, Aso-no-Ōkami is seen as protecting worshippers from traffic accidents and other untoward events.<ref name="jnto1">{{cite web|title=Aso-jinja Shrine|url=http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/attractions/facilities/spots/shrines_temples/83dn3a000000ek1x.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171015222732/http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/attractions/facilities/spots/shrines_temples/83dn3a000000ek1x.html|archive-date=2017-10-15|website=[[Japan National Tourist Organization|JNTO]]}}</ref>
[[Yabusame]] is an annual festival which brings together horse-mounted archers, special arrows and targets, and Shinto ritual at Aso Shrine.<ref>[http://edpas.net/journal/109/ Yabusame at Aso Shrine] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081204191951/http://edpas.net/journal/109/|date=December 4, 2008}}</ref>
The ''Aso no Himatsuri'' festival has its origin in the month of March festivals such as ''Aso no Noyaki'' (the first burning in Aso) and ''Aso jinja no Hifuri shinji'' (the fire ritual of Aso Shrine).<ref>[http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/ JAL Guide to Japan:] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061026103601/http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/|date=2006-10-26}} [http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/city_information/fuk/ Fukuoaka]; {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061026165358/http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/city_information/fuk/|date=2006-10-26}} JNTO: [http://www.iexplore.com/dmap/Japan/Event/16312 Fire Festivals.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607060650/http://www.iexplore.com/dmap/Japan/Event/16312|date=June 7, 2011}}</ref> Although rarely performed today, ceremonies which honor ancestors who settled near the [[Aso Caldera|Aso caldera]] do continue to be associated with the Aso jinja.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Akimoto|first1=Kazuhide|last2=Nakamura|first2=Minako|date=November 15, 2008|title=Settlement Composition and Actual Condition of Grave Festivals in Aso Caldera Settlements|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.3130/jaabe.7.209|journal=Journal of Asian Architecture and Building Engineering|volume=7|issue=2|pages=209-216|doi=10.3130/jaabe.7.209|doi-access=free}}</ref>
=== Deities === [[File:Origin_of_Iwato_Kagura_Dance_Amaterasu_by_Toyokuni_III_(Kunisada)_1856.png|thumb|The Goddess ''Amaterasu'' is said to be the source of ''Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto's'' divine powers, as her descendant.|259x259px]] The shrine's main kami is ''Ichinomiya Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto'' (一の宮健磐龍命) the creator of [[Aso, Kumamoto|Aso]] and the God credited with teaching the villagers about agriculture. He is said to be the descendant of Emperor Jinmu. Since Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto was descended from Emperor Jinmu who is said to have been human, legends surrounding his divinity is unclear. Some state that through his lineage from the Goddess [[Amaterasu]] he was given divine powers for creating Aso. Another legend states that the deity of the volcano, entered the body of Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto turning him from a human into a divine being. These are common folklore among the people with the only consensus being that over time, the deity of the land and the deity of the volcano was combined into one symbol by the name of ''Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto''.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014" />
The second important deity is called ''Ninomiya Aso-tsu-hime-no-mikoto'' the wife of ''Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto'' (二の宮阿蘇都媛命).
The third important deity mentioned is ''Juuichinomiya Kuni-no-miyatsuko-hayamikatama-no-mikoto'' (十一の宮園造速瓶玉命).
The other deities are the kami of fire 火の神, the kami of water 水の神 flowing near the ''rōmon'' gate of the shrine and the other kami of agriculture 農の神.
=== U-no-matsuri === The Aso shrine's ''U-no-matsuri'' (卯の祭) is a 13-day event that occurs in March to welcome spring and pray for the beginning of the rice planting season. The U-no-matsuri marks the anniversary of Aso shrine's chief deity ''Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto's'' arrival in Aso. This event occurred in the second month of the lunar calendar which is March in the current calendar. The shrine's Guuji San perform sacred Shinto music and dances every day of the festival while praying for a rich harvest.<ref name="Takano-2006" />
Occurring simultaneously to the U-no-matsuri, is a prominent festival called the ''Tazukuri Matsuri'' (田作り祭り) which is celebrated over 7 days, and the ''Daihimonjiyaki'' (大火文字焼き) which is the lighting of the Chinese characters for "fire" and "flame" on the mountains which is also done around the same time and sometimes the same day as the Tazukuri Matsuri.<ref name="末吉-2018">{{Cite book|title=肥後一の宮阿蘇神社|last=末吉|first=駿一|publisher=(株）マインド|year=2018|pages=38, 39, 40 and 43}}</ref>

[[File:Tennō Jimmu.jpg|thumb|248x248px|Emperor Jimmu, who is said to be an ancestor of Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto.]] ==Worship== Aso-no-Ōkami, the ''[[kami]]'' or spirit who is believed to dwell at Aso Shrine has been worshipped from early times{{vague|date=November 2014}} as the guardian deity of safety in navigation, and today, Aso-no-Ōkami is seen as protecting worshippers from traffic accidents and other untoward events.<ref name="jnto1">{{cite web|title=Aso-jinja Shrine|url=http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/attractions/facilities/spots/shrines_temples/83dn3a000000ek1x.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171015222732/http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/attractions/facilities/spots/shrines_temples/83dn3a000000ek1x.html|archive-date=2017-10-15|website=[[Japan National Tourist Organization|JNTO]]}}</ref>
[[Yabusame]] is an annual festival which brings together horse-mounted archers, special arrows and targets, and Shinto ritual at Aso Shrine.<ref>[http://edpas.net/journal/109/ Yabusame at Aso Shrine] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081204191951/http://edpas.net/journal/109/|date=December 4, 2008}}</ref>
The ''Aso no Himatsuri'' festival has its origin in the month of March festivals such as ''Aso no Noyaki'' (the first burning in Aso) and ''Aso jinja no Hifuri shinji'' (the fire ritual of Aso Shrine).<ref>[http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/ JAL Guide to Japan:] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061026103601/http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/|date=2006-10-26}} [http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/city_information/fuk/ Fukuoaka]; {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061026165358/http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/city_information/fuk/|date=2006-10-26}} JNTO: [http://www.iexplore.com/dmap/Japan/Event/16312 Fire Festivals.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607060650/http://www.iexplore.com/dmap/Japan/Event/16312|date=June 7, 2011}}</ref> Although rarely performed today, ceremonies which honor ancestors who settled near the [[Aso Caldera|Aso caldera]] do continue to be associated with the Aso jinja.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Akimoto|first1=Kazuhide|last2=Nakamura|first2=Minako|date=November 15, 2008|title=Settlement Composition and Actual Condition of Grave Festivals in Aso Caldera Settlements|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.3130/jaabe.7.209|journal=Journal of Asian Architecture and Building Engineering|volume=7|issue=2|pages=209-216|doi=10.3130/jaabe.7.209|doi-access=free}}</ref>
=== Deities === [[File:Origin_of_Iwato_Kagura_Dance_Amaterasu_by_Toyokuni_III_(Kunisada)_1856.png|thumb|The Goddess ''Amaterasu'' is said to be the source of ''Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto's'' divine powers, as her descendant.|259x259px]] The shrine's main kami is ''Ichinomiya Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto'' (一の宮健磐龍命) the creator of [[Aso, Kumamoto|Aso]] and the God credited with teaching the villagers about agriculture. He is said to be the descendant of Emperor Jinmu. Since Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto was descended from Emperor Jinmu who is said to have been human, legends surrounding his divinity is unclear. Some state that through his lineage from the Goddess [[Amaterasu]] he was given divine powers for creating Aso. Another legend states that the deity of the volcano, entered the body of Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto turning him from a human into a divine being. These are common folklore among the people with the only consensus being that over time, the deity of the land and the deity of the volcano was combined into one symbol by the name of ''Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto''.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014" />
The second important deity is called ''Ninomiya Aso-tsu-hime-no-mikoto'' the wife of ''Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto'' (二の宮阿蘇都媛命).
The third important deity mentioned is ''Juuichinomiya Kuni-no-miyatsuko-hayamikatama-no-mikoto'' (十一の宮園造速瓶玉命).
The other deities are the kami of fire 火の神, the kami of water 水の神 flowing near the ''rōmon'' gate of the shrine and the other kami of agriculture 農の神.
=== U-no-matsuri === The Aso shrine's ''U-no-matsuri'' (卯の祭) is a 13-day event that occurs in March to welcome spring and pray for the beginning of the rice planting season. The U-no-matsuri marks the anniversary of Aso shrine's chief deity ''Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto's'' arrival in Aso. This event occurred in the second month of the lunar calendar which is March in the current calendar. The shrine's Guuji San perform sacred Shinto music and dances every day of the festival while praying for a rich harvest.<ref name="Takano-2006" />
Occurring simultaneously to the U-no-matsuri, is a prominent festival called the ''Tazukuri Matsuri'' (田作り祭り) which is celebrated over 7 days, and the ''Daihimonjiyaki'' (大火文字焼き) which is the lighting of the Chinese characters for "fire" and "flame" on the mountains which is also done around the same time and sometimes the same day as the Tazukuri Matsuri.<ref name="末吉-2018">{{Cite book|title=肥後一の宮阿蘇神社|last=末吉|first=駿一|publisher=(株）マインド|year=2018|pages=38, 39, 40 and 43}}</ref>

[[en:Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto]] {{draft}} {{Infobox noble|reign-type=[[神武天皇]]の[[皇子]]|birth_date=unknown|father=[[Kamuyaimimi]]|name=Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto|spouse=Asotsuhime no Mikoto|issue=Hayamikatama no Mikoto | reign-type = [[神武天皇]]の[[皇子]] | birth_date = unknown | father = {{ill|Kamuyaimimi|en}} | name = Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto | spouse = Asotsuhime no Mikoto | issue = Hayamikatama no Mikoto | père = {{ill|Kamuyaimimi|en}} | conjoint1 = Asotsuhime no Mikoto | enfants1 = Hayamikatama no Mikoto | image = 阿蘇神社02 Aso shrine - panoramio.jpg }}
Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto is a Japanese kami worshipped at [[Aso Shrine]]. He is a grandson of Jimmu.<ref name="Ponsonby">Ponsonby-Fane, ''Shrines,'' pp. 480-484.</ref>
He is the son of [[Kamuyaimimi]]<ref name="Takano-2006" />, and grandson of [[Jimmu]].<ref name="Ponsonby" />
[[ja:健磐龍命]]
He is the {{ill|Oyagami|en}} of the {{ill|Aso clan|en|Aso clan}}.<ref name="Takano-2006" />
== Mythological background == He is the son of [[Kamuyaimimi]]<ref name="Takano-2006" />, and grandson of [[Jimmu]].<ref name="Ponsonby" />
The shrine is dedicated to the veneration of [[Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto]] (健磐龍命), who was a grandson of Japan's first emperor and the nephew of [[Emperor Suizei]], the second monarch on the traditional list of emperors.<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' p. 29.</ref> In the same period that [[Emperor Jimmu]] was establishing his palace at [[Kashihara]] at the foot of [[Yamato Sanzan|Mount Unebi]] in [[Yamato Province|Yamato province]],<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, ''Imperial House,'' p. 28; [http://www.kunaicho.go.jp/ryobo/guide/001/index.html ''Unebiyama-no Ushitora-no-sumi-no misasagi'' (''Unebi Goryō,'' tomb of Emperor Jimmu).]</ref> Takeiwatasu was sent to Aso where he helped establish a number of agricultural communities; and later, he is said to have built a palace at [[Miyagi Prefecture|Miyagi]].<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, ''Shrines,'' pp. 480-484.</ref>
=== The creation of Aso === [[File:Ojodake.jpg|thumb|Ojodake on Mt. Aso where ''Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto'' practised his archery.]] According to an interview with several priests at Aso shrine, the legend of Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto and the formation of Aso City, is as follows:
Thousands of years ago, the crater now known as Aso city was said to be filled with water and was thereby a huge lake surrounded by the outer rim of the caldera. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto kicked in the western side of the caldera<ref name="Takano-2006" /> at what is now known as [[Tateno Station (Kumamoto)|Tateno]], [[Minamiaso, Kumamoto|Minami-Aso]]. He fell from the effort and was unable to stand for a while hence the name "Tateno" meaning "''unable to stand up''."As the water drained away forming rivers on the outside of the valley, a huge catfish (''[[Namazu (Japanese mythology)|Namazu]])'' appeared. The catfish was settled at the bottom of the lake where some stories say it was asked to leave by Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. The catfish went to Namazu, [[Kashima, Kumamoto|Kashima]] where Namazu-sha Shrine was established to pay homage to the soul of the catfish as the spirit of the lake. Now the shrine is in the precincts of the Kokuzo Shrine.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014">{{Cite news|date=2014|title=The Deity of the Volcano Geosite|work=Aso GeoPark Geosite Map|publisher=Aso Local Development Design Centre Foundation|type=Guide Map|url=http://www.aso-geopark.jp/}}</ref> [[File:Matoishi.jpg|thumb|The ''Matoishi'' (target stone) that Kihachi was sent to, to retrieve the arrows for Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto.]]
=== The legend of Kihachi === The legend of Kihachi surrounds the Hitaki-Shinji festival commemorated in Aso annually. Legend states that Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto liked practicing his archery. He would stand on Ojodake (a cone shaped formation on Mt. Aso) and practice shooting ''matoishi'' (target stone) in what is now Matoishi in Aso, located north of the caldera. Kihachi his servant, was in charge of bringing the arrows back from the ''matoishi'' to Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. After the 100th arrow was shot, Kihachi got tired and kicked the arrow back breaking it in half. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto was furious and drawing his sword slayed Kihachi cutting off his head. Kihachi's head ascended as a deity vowing to exact revenge on Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto's village of Aso. Later, during the winter months it frosted in Aso valley damaging all of the crops. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto realised that this was the revenge that Kihachi had spoken of and so he enshrined his soul at ''Shimo Shrine'' (''frost shrine'') to abate his anger. A ritual called the Hitaki-Shinji was started where a fire is kept for 2 months to pray for a good harvest and prevent frost damage to the crops.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014" /> They say that this is why the winters in Aso are so cold.
=== Hereditary succession === The position of Chief Priest of Aso Shrine is hereditary and is passed down from generation to generation with the oldest male in the family becoming the new head of the shrine. The Aso family has the second oldest recorded lineage in Japan after the Imperial family. The family themselves are said to be descendants of Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. The Aso family were priests but also rose to power as a powerful samurai clan in the 11th century. They remained in prominence until the 16th century as their feudal lord continued to rule over half of what is now known as Kumamoto Prefecture. This contributed economically to the family and the shrine, allowing them to rebuild shrine buildings and hold festivals. It also made it possible for them to establish branches of the Aso shrine in other locations. Some of those shrines still remain in up to 500 locations to this day. Koreyuki Aso (''Aso Koreyuki in Japanese name order'') was the 91st Chief Priest of Aso Shrine with his son being the 92nd.<ref name="Takano-2006">{{Cite book|title=History and Festivals of the Aso Shrine|last1=Takano|first1=Tomoaki|last2=Uchimura|first2=Hiroaki|publisher=Aso Shrine|year=2006|location=Aso Shrine, Ichinomiya, Aso City.}}</ref>

[[en:Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto]] {{draft}} {{Infobox noble|reign-type=[[神武天皇]]の[[皇子]]|birth_date=unknown|father={{ill|Kamuyaimimi|en}}|name=Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto|spouse=Asotsuhime no Mikoto|issue=Hayamikatama no Mikoto | père = {{ill|Kamuyaimimi|en}} | conjoint1 = Asotsuhime no Mikoto | enfants1 = Hayamikatama no Mikoto | image = 阿蘇神社02 Aso shrine - panoramio.jpg |caption={{ill|Aso shrine|en}}, his main cult center}}
Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto is a Japanese kami worshipped at [[Aso Shrine]]. He is a grandson of Jimmu.<ref name="Ponsonby">Ponsonby-Fane, ''Shrines,'' pp. 480-484.</ref>
He is the son of [[Kamuyaimimi]]<ref name="Takano-2006" />, and grandson of [[Jimmu]].<ref name="Ponsonby" />
[[ja:健磐龍命]]
He is the {{ill|Oyagami|en}} of the {{ill|Aso clan|en|Aso clan}}.<ref name="Takano-2006" />
== Mythological background == He is the son of [[Kamuyaimimi]]<ref name="Takano-2006" />, and grandson of [[Jimmu]].<ref name="Ponsonby" />
The shrine is dedicated to the veneration of [[Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto]] (健磐龍命), who was a grandson of Japan's first emperor and the nephew of [[Emperor Suizei]], the second monarch on the traditional list of emperors.<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' p. 29.</ref> In the same period that [[Emperor Jimmu]] was establishing his palace at [[Kashihara]] at the foot of [[Yamato Sanzan|Mount Unebi]] in [[Yamato Province|Yamato province]],<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, ''Imperial House,'' p. 28; [http://www.kunaicho.go.jp/ryobo/guide/001/index.html ''Unebiyama-no Ushitora-no-sumi-no misasagi'' (''Unebi Goryō,'' tomb of Emperor Jimmu).]</ref> Takeiwatasu was sent to Aso where he helped establish a number of agricultural communities; and later, he is said to have built a palace at [[Miyagi Prefecture|Miyagi]].<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, ''Shrines,'' pp. 480-484.</ref>
=== The creation of Aso === [[File:Ojodake.jpg|thumb|Ojodake on Mt. Aso where ''Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto'' practised his archery.]] According to an interview with several priests at Aso shrine, the legend of Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto and the formation of Aso City, is as follows:
Thousands of years ago, the crater now known as Aso city was said to be filled with water and was thereby a huge lake surrounded by the outer rim of the caldera. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto kicked in the western side of the caldera<ref name="Takano-2006" /> at what is now known as [[Tateno Station (Kumamoto)|Tateno]], [[Minamiaso, Kumamoto|Minami-Aso]]. He fell from the effort and was unable to stand for a while hence the name "Tateno" meaning "''unable to stand up''."As the water drained away forming rivers on the outside of the valley, a huge catfish (''[[Namazu (Japanese mythology)|Namazu]])'' appeared. The catfish was settled at the bottom of the lake where some stories say it was asked to leave by Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. The catfish went to Namazu, [[Kashima, Kumamoto|Kashima]] where Namazu-sha Shrine was established to pay homage to the soul of the catfish as the spirit of the lake. Now the shrine is in the precincts of the Kokuzo Shrine.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014">{{Cite news|date=2014|title=The Deity of the Volcano Geosite|work=Aso GeoPark Geosite Map|publisher=Aso Local Development Design Centre Foundation|type=Guide Map|url=http://www.aso-geopark.jp/}}</ref> [[File:Matoishi.jpg|thumb|The ''Matoishi'' (target stone) that Kihachi was sent to, to retrieve the arrows for Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto.]]
=== The legend of Kihachi === The legend of Kihachi surrounds the Hitaki-Shinji festival commemorated in Aso annually. Legend states that Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto liked practicing his archery. He would stand on Ojodake (a cone shaped formation on Mt. Aso) and practice shooting ''matoishi'' (target stone) in what is now Matoishi in Aso, located north of the caldera. Kihachi his servant, was in charge of bringing the arrows back from the ''matoishi'' to Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. After the 100th arrow was shot, Kihachi got tired and kicked the arrow back breaking it in half. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto was furious and drawing his sword slayed Kihachi cutting off his head. Kihachi's head ascended as a deity vowing to exact revenge on Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto's village of Aso. Later, during the winter months it frosted in Aso valley damaging all of the crops. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto realised that this was the revenge that Kihachi had spoken of and so he enshrined his soul at ''Shimo Shrine'' (''frost shrine'') to abate his anger. A ritual called the Hitaki-Shinji was started where a fire is kept for 2 months to pray for a good harvest and prevent frost damage to the crops.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014" /> They say that this is why the winters in Aso are so cold.
=== Hereditary succession === The position of Chief Priest of Aso Shrine is hereditary and is passed down from generation to generation with the oldest male in the family becoming the new head of the shrine. The Aso family has the second oldest recorded lineage in Japan after the Imperial family. The family themselves are said to be descendants of Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. The Aso family were priests but also rose to power as a powerful samurai clan in the 11th century. They remained in prominence until the 16th century as their feudal lord continued to rule over half of what is now known as Kumamoto Prefecture. This contributed economically to the family and the shrine, allowing them to rebuild shrine buildings and hold festivals. It also made it possible for them to establish branches of the Aso shrine in other locations. Some of those shrines still remain in up to 500 locations to this day. Koreyuki Aso (''Aso Koreyuki in Japanese name order'') was the 91st Chief Priest of Aso Shrine with his son being the 92nd.<ref name="Takano-2006">{{Cite book|title=History and Festivals of the Aso Shrine|last1=Takano|first1=Tomoaki|last2=Uchimura|first2=Hiroaki|publisher=Aso Shrine|year=2006|location=Aso Shrine, Ichinomiya, Aso City.}}</ref>

[[File:Tennō Jimmu.jpg|thumb|248x248px|Emperor Jimmu, who is said to be an ancestor of Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto.]] ==Worship== Aso-no-Ōkami, the ''[[kami]]'' or spirit who is believed to dwell at Aso Shrine has been worshipped from early times{{vague|date=November 2014}} as the guardian deity of safety in navigation, and today, Aso-no-Ōkami is seen as protecting worshippers from traffic accidents and other untoward events.<ref name="jnto1">{{cite web|title=Aso-jinja Shrine|url=http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/attractions/facilities/spots/shrines_temples/83dn3a000000ek1x.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171015222732/http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/attractions/facilities/spots/shrines_temples/83dn3a000000ek1x.html|archive-date=2017-10-15|website=[[Japan National Tourist Organization|JNTO]]}}</ref>
[[Yabusame]] is an annual festival which brings together horse-mounted archers, special arrows and targets, and Shinto ritual at Aso Shrine.<ref>[http://edpas.net/journal/109/ Yabusame at Aso Shrine] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081204191951/http://edpas.net/journal/109/|date=December 4, 2008}}</ref>
The ''Aso no Himatsuri'' festival has its origin in the month of March festivals such as ''Aso no Noyaki'' (the first burning in Aso) and ''Aso jinja no Hifuri shinji'' (the fire ritual of Aso Shrine).<ref>[http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/ JAL Guide to Japan:] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061026103601/http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/|date=2006-10-26}} [http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/city_information/fuk/ Fukuoaka]; {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061026165358/http://www.gu.jal.com/world/en/guidetojapan/city_information/fuk/|date=2006-10-26}} JNTO: [http://www.iexplore.com/dmap/Japan/Event/16312 Fire Festivals.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607060650/http://www.iexplore.com/dmap/Japan/Event/16312|date=June 7, 2011}}</ref> Although rarely performed today, ceremonies which honor ancestors who settled near the [[Aso Caldera|Aso caldera]] do continue to be associated with the Aso jinja.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Akimoto|first1=Kazuhide|last2=Nakamura|first2=Minako|date=November 15, 2008|title=Settlement Composition and Actual Condition of Grave Festivals in Aso Caldera Settlements|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.3130/jaabe.7.209|journal=Journal of Asian Architecture and Building Engineering|volume=7|issue=2|pages=209-216|doi=10.3130/jaabe.7.209|doi-access=free}}</ref>
=== Deities === [[File:Origin_of_Iwato_Kagura_Dance_Amaterasu_by_Toyokuni_III_(Kunisada)_1856.png|thumb|The Goddess ''Amaterasu'' is said to be the source of ''Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto's'' divine powers, as her descendant.|259x259px]] The shrine's main kami is ''Ichinomiya Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto'' (一の宮健磐龍命) the creator of [[Aso, Kumamoto|Aso]] and the God credited with teaching the villagers about agriculture. He is said to be the descendant of Emperor Jinmu. Since Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto was descended from Emperor Jinmu who is said to have been human, legends surrounding his divinity is unclear. Some state that through his lineage from the Goddess [[Amaterasu]] he was given divine powers for creating Aso. Another legend states that the deity of the volcano, entered the body of Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto turning him from a human into a divine being. These are common folklore among the people with the only consensus being that over time, the deity of the land and the deity of the volcano was combined into one symbol by the name of ''Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto''.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014" />
The second important deity is called ''Ninomiya Aso-tsu-hime-no-mikoto'' the wife of ''Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto'' (二の宮阿蘇都媛命).
The third important deity mentioned is ''Juuichinomiya Kuni-no-miyatsuko-hayamikatama-no-mikoto'' (十一の宮園造速瓶玉命).
The other deities are the kami of fire 火の神, the kami of water 水の神 flowing near the ''rōmon'' gate of the shrine and the other kami of agriculture 農の神.
=== U-no-matsuri === The Aso shrine's ''U-no-matsuri'' (卯の祭) is a 13-day event that occurs in March to welcome spring and pray for the beginning of the rice planting season. The U-no-matsuri marks the anniversary of Aso shrine's chief deity ''Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto's'' arrival in Aso. This event occurred in the second month of the lunar calendar which is March in the current calendar. The shrine's Guuji San perform sacred Shinto music and dances every day of the festival while praying for a rich harvest.<ref name="Takano-2006" />
Occurring simultaneously to the U-no-matsuri, is a prominent festival called the ''Tazukuri Matsuri'' (田作り祭り) which is celebrated over 7 days, and the ''Daihimonjiyaki'' (大火文字焼き) which is the lighting of the Chinese characters for "fire" and "flame" on the mountains which is also done around the same time and sometimes the same day as the Tazukuri Matsuri.<ref name="末吉-2018">{{Cite book|title=肥後一の宮阿蘇神社|last=末吉|first=駿一|publisher=(株）マインド|year=2018|pages=38, 39, 40 and 43}}</ref>

=== Deities === The shrine's main kami is ''Ichinomiya Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto'' (一の宮健磐龍命) the creator of [[Aso, Kumamoto|Aso]] and the God credited with teaching the villagers about agriculture. === U-no-matsuri === The Aso shrine's ''U-no-matsuri'' (卯の祭) is a 13-day event that occurs in March to welcome spring and pray for the beginning of the rice planting season. This event occurred in the second month of the lunar calendar which is March in the current calendar. The shrine's Guuji San perform sacred Shinto music and dances every day of the festival while praying for a rich harvest.<ref name="Takano-2006" />

[[en:Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto]] {{draft}} {{Infobox noble|reign-type=[[神武天皇]]の[[皇子]]|birth_date=unknown|father={{ill|Kamuyaimimi|en}}|name=Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto|spouse=Asotsuhime no Mikoto|issue=Hayamikatama no Mikoto | père = {{ill|Kamuyaimimi|en}} | conjoint1 = Asotsuhime no Mikoto | enfants1 = Hayamikatama no Mikoto | image = 阿蘇神社02 Aso shrine - panoramio.jpg |caption={{ill|Aso shrine|en}}, his main cult center}}
Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto is a Japanese kami worshipped at [[Aso Shrine]]. He is a grandson of Jimmu.<ref name="Ponsonby">Ponsonby-Fane, ''Shrines,'' pp. 480-484.</ref>
He is the son of [[Kamuyaimimi]]<ref name="Takano-2006" />, and grandson of [[Jimmu]].<ref name="Ponsonby" />
[[ja:健磐龍命]]
He is the {{ill|Oyagami|en}} of the {{ill|Aso clan|en|Aso clan}}.<ref name="Takano-2006" />
He is an agricultural god, and it is traditionally believed the people of [[Aso, Kumamoto]] could not farm until he taught them how.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014" />
== Mythological background == He is the son of [[Kamuyaimimi]]<ref name="Takano-2006" />, and grandson of [[Jimmu]].<ref name="Ponsonby" />
The shrine is dedicated to the veneration of [[Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto]] (健磐龍命), who was a grandson of Japan's first emperor and the nephew of [[Emperor Suizei]], the second monarch on the traditional list of emperors.<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' p. 29.</ref> In the same period that [[Emperor Jimmu]] was establishing his palace at [[Kashihara]] at the foot of [[Yamato Sanzan|Mount Unebi]] in [[Yamato Province|Yamato province]],<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, ''Imperial House,'' p. 28; [http://www.kunaicho.go.jp/ryobo/guide/001/index.html ''Unebiyama-no Ushitora-no-sumi-no misasagi'' (''Unebi Goryō,'' tomb of Emperor Jimmu).]</ref> Takeiwatasu was sent to Aso where he helped establish a number of agricultural communities; and later, he is said to have built a palace at [[Miyagi Prefecture|Miyagi]].<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, ''Shrines,'' pp. 480-484.</ref>
=== The creation of Aso === [[File:Ojodake.jpg|thumb|Ojodake on Mt. Aso where ''Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto'' practised his archery.]] According to an interview with several priests at Aso shrine, the legend of Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto and the formation of Aso City, is as follows:
Thousands of years ago, the crater now known as Aso city was said to be filled with water and was thereby a huge lake surrounded by the outer rim of the {{ill|Aso Caldera|lt=caldera|en|Aso Caldera}}. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto kicked in the western side of the {{ill|Aso Caldera|lt=caldera|en|Aso Caldera}}<ref name="Takano-2006" /> at what is now known as [[Tateno Station (Kumamoto)|Tateno]], [[Minamiaso, Kumamoto|Minami-Aso]]. He fell from the effort and was unable to stand for a while hence the name "Tateno" meaning "''unable to stand up''."As the water drained away forming rivers on the outside of the valley, a huge catfish (''[[Namazu (Japanese mythology)|Namazu]])'' appeared. The catfish was settled at the bottom of the lake where some stories say it was asked to leave by Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. The catfish went to Namazu, [[Kashima, Kumamoto|Kashima]] where Namazu-sha Shrine was established to pay homage to the soul of the catfish as the spirit of the lake. Now the shrine is in the precincts of the Kokuzo Shrine.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014">{{Cite news|date=2014|title=The Deity of the Volcano Geosite|work=Aso GeoPark Geosite Map|publisher=Aso Local Development Design Centre Foundation|type=Guide Map|url=http://www.aso-geopark.jp/}}</ref> [[File:Matoishi.jpg|thumb|The ''Matoishi'' (target stone) that Kihachi was sent to, to retrieve the arrows for Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto.]]
=== The legend of Kihachi === The legend of Kihachi surrounds the Hitaki-Shinji festival commemorated in Aso annually. Legend states that Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto liked practicing his archery. He would stand on Ojodake (a cone shaped formation on Mt. Aso) and practice shooting ''matoishi'' (target stone) in what is now Matoishi in Aso, located north of the {{ill|Aso Caldera|lt=caldera|en|Aso Caldera}}. Kihachi his servant, was in charge of bringing the arrows back from the ''matoishi'' to Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. After the 100th arrow was shot, Kihachi got tired and kicked the arrow back breaking it in half. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto was furious and drawing his sword slayed Kihachi cutting off his head. Kihachi's head ascended as a deity vowing to exact revenge on Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto's village of Aso. Later, during the winter months it frosted in Aso valley damaging all of the crops. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto realised that this was the revenge that Kihachi had spoken of and so he enshrined his soul at ''Shimo Shrine'' (''frost shrine'') to abate his anger. A ritual called the Hitaki-Shinji was started where a fire is kept for 2 months to pray for a good harvest and prevent frost damage to the crops.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014" /> They say that this is why the winters in Aso are so cold.
=== Hereditary succession === The position of Chief Priest of Aso Shrine is hereditary and is passed down from generation to generation with the oldest male in the family becoming the new head of the shrine. The Aso family has the second oldest recorded lineage in Japan after the Imperial family. The family themselves are said to be descendants of Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. The Aso family were priests but also rose to power as a powerful samurai clan in the 11th century. They remained in prominence until the 16th century as their feudal lord continued to rule over half of what is now known as Kumamoto Prefecture. This contributed economically to the family and the shrine, allowing them to rebuild shrine buildings and hold festivals. It also made it possible for them to establish branches of the Aso shrine in other locations. Some of those shrines still remain in up to 500 locations to this day. Koreyuki Aso (''Aso Koreyuki in Japanese name order'') was the 91st Chief Priest of Aso Shrine with his son being the 92nd.<ref name="Takano-2006">{{Cite book|title=History and Festivals of the Aso Shrine|last1=Takano|first1=Tomoaki|last2=Uchimura|first2=Hiroaki|publisher=Aso Shrine|year=2006|location=Aso Shrine, Ichinomiya, Aso City.}}</ref>

The shrine is dedicated to the veneration of [[Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto]] (健磐龍命), who was a grandson of Japan's first emperor and the nephew of [[Emperor Suizei]], the second monarch on the traditional list of emperors.<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, Richard. (1959). ''The Imperial House of Japan,'' p. 29.</ref> In the same period that [[Emperor Jimmu]] was establishing his palace at [[Kashihara]] at the foot of [[Yamato Sanzan|Mount Unebi]] in [[Yamato Province|Yamato province]],<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, ''Imperial House,'' p. 28; [http://www.kunaicho.go.jp/ryobo/guide/001/index.html ''Unebiyama-no Ushitora-no-sumi-no misasagi'' (''Unebi Goryō,'' tomb of Emperor Jimmu).]</ref> Takeiwatasu was sent to Aso where he helped establish a number of agricultural communities; and later, he is said to have built a palace at [[Miyagi Prefecture|Miyagi]].<ref>Ponsonby-Fane, ''Shrines,'' pp. 480-484.</ref>

Thousands of years ago, the crater now known as Aso city was said to be filled with water and was thereby a huge lake surrounded by the outer rim of the {{ill|Aso Caldera|lt=caldera|en|Aso Caldera}}. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto kicked in the western side of the {{ill|Aso Caldera|lt=caldera|en|Aso Caldera}}<ref name="Takano-2006" /> at what is now known as [[Tateno Station (Kumamoto)|Tateno]], [[Minamiaso, Kumamoto|Minami-Aso]]. He fell from the effort and was unable to stand for a while hence the name "Tateno" meaning "''unable to stand up''."As the water drained away forming rivers on the outside of the valley, a huge catfish (''[[Namazu (Japanese mythology)|Namazu]])'' appeared. The catfish was settled at the bottom of the lake where some stories say it was asked to leave by Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. The catfish went to Namazu, [[Kashima, Kumamoto|Kashima]] where Namazu-sha Shrine was established to pay homage to the soul of the catfish as the spirit of the lake. Now the shrine is in the precincts of the Kokuzo Shrine.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014">{{Cite news|date=2014|title=The Deity of the Volcano Geosite|work=Aso GeoPark Geosite Map|publisher=Aso Local Development Design Centre Foundation|type=Guide Map|url=http://www.aso-geopark.jp/}}</ref> [[File:Matoishi.jpg|thumb|The ''Matoishi'' (target stone) that Kihachi was sent to, to retrieve the arrows for Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto.]]
=== The legend of Kihachi === The legend of Kihachi surrounds the Hitaki-Shinji festival commemorated in Aso annually. Legend states that Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto liked practicing his archery. He would stand on Ojodake (a cone shaped formation on Mt. Aso) and practice shooting ''matoishi'' (target stone) in what is now Matoishi in Aso, located north of the {{ill|Aso Caldera|lt=caldera|en|Aso Caldera}}. Kihachi his servant, was in charge of bringing the arrows back from the ''matoishi'' to Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. After the 100th arrow was shot, Kihachi got tired and kicked the arrow back breaking it in half. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto was furious and drawing his sword slayed Kihachi cutting off his head. Kihachi's head ascended as a deity vowing to exact revenge on Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto's village of Aso. Later, during the winter months it frosted in Aso valley damaging all of the crops. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto realised that this was the revenge that Kihachi had spoken of and so he enshrined his soul at ''Shimo Shrine'' (''frost shrine'') to abate his anger. A ritual called the Hitaki-Shinji was started where a fire is kept for 2 months to pray for a good harvest and prevent frost damage to the crops.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014" /> They say that this is why the winters in Aso are so cold.

This contributed economically to the family and the shrine, allowing them to rebuild shrine buildings and hold festivals. It also made it possible for them to establish branches of the Aso shrine in other locations. Some of those shrines still remain in up to 500 locations to this day. Koreyuki Aso (''Aso Koreyuki in Japanese name order'') was the 91st Chief Priest of Aso Shrine with his son being the 92nd.<ref name="Takano-2006">{{Cite book|title=History and Festivals of the Aso Shrine|last1=Takano|first1=Tomoaki|last2=Uchimura|first2=Hiroaki|publisher=Aso Shrine|year=2006|location=Aso Shrine, Ichinomiya, Aso City.}}</ref>

He is said to be the descendant of Emperor Jinmu. Since Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto was descended from Emperor Jinmu who is said to have been human, legends surrounding his divinity is unclear. Some state that through his lineage from the Goddess [[Amaterasu]] he was given divine powers for creating Aso. Another legend states that the deity of the volcano, entered the body of Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto turning him from a human into a divine being. These are common folklore among the people with the only consensus being that over time, the deity of the land and the deity of the volcano was combined into one symbol by the name of ''Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto''.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014" /> [[File:Matoishi.jpg|thumb|The ''Matoishi'' (target stone) that Kihachi was sent to, to retrieve the arrows for Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto.]]
=== The legend of Kihachi === The legend of Kihachi surrounds the Hitaki-Shinji festival commemorated in Aso annually. Legend states that Takeiwatatsu-no-mikoto liked practicing his archery. He would stand on Ojodake (a cone shaped formation on Mt. Aso) and practice shooting ''matoishi'' (target stone) in what is now Matoishi in Aso, located north of the {{ill|Aso Caldera|lt=caldera|en|Aso Caldera}}. Kihachi his servant, was in charge of bringing the arrows back from the ''matoishi'' to Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. After the 100th arrow was shot, Kihachi got tired and kicked the arrow back breaking it in half. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto was furious and drawing his sword slayed Kihachi cutting off his head. Kihachi's head ascended as a deity vowing to exact revenge on Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto's village of Aso. Later, during the winter months it frosted in Aso valley damaging all of the crops. Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto realised that this was the revenge that Kihachi had spoken of and so he enshrined his soul at ''Shimo Shrine'' (''frost shrine'') to abate his anger. A ritual called the Hitaki-Shinji was started where a fire is kept for 2 months to pray for a good harvest and prevent frost damage to the crops.<ref name="Aso GeoPark Geosite Map-2014" /> They say that this is why the winters in Aso are so cold.
=== Hereditary succession === The position of Chief Priest of Aso Shrine is hereditary and is passed down from generation to generation with the oldest male in the family becoming the new head of the shrine. The Aso family has the second oldest recorded lineage in Japan after the Imperial family. The family themselves are said to be descendants of Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto. The Aso family were priests but also rose to power as a powerful samurai clan in the 11th century. They remained in prominence until the 16th century as their feudal lord continued to rule over half of what is now known as Kumamoto Prefecture. This contributed economically to the family and the shrine, allowing them to rebuild shrine buildings and hold festivals. It also made it possible for them to establish branches of the Aso shrine in other locations. Some of those shrines still remain in up to 500 locations to this day. Koreyuki Aso (''Aso Koreyuki in Japanese name order'') was the 91st Chief Priest of Aso Shrine with his son being the 92nd.<ref name="Takano-2006">{{Cite book|title=History and Festivals of the Aso Shrine|last1=Takano|first1=Tomoaki|last2=Uchimura|first2=Hiroaki|publisher=Aso Shrine|year=2006|location=Aso Shrine, Ichinomiya, Aso City.}}</ref>
{{Tree chart/start|align=center|summary=Aso family tree}} {{Tree chart| | | | | |EmJ|EmJ=[[Emperor Jimmu]]|}} {{Tree chart| | |,|-|-|-|+|-|-|-|.| }} {{Tree chart| |MOM||DAD| |DAISY|y| Lee|MOM=Kanakori no Kami |DAD={{ill|Kamuyaimimi|lt=Kamuyaimimi no Mikoto|simple}}|DAISY=Kunitatsu no Kami |Lee=Hime Miko no Kami|}} {{Tree chart| ||!| | | |!| | | | ,| -|^|- |.|}} {{Tree chart| |Koutou | | ME |y | SIS | |SHIN|y|YAYA| |Koutou=Imperial Family Line|ME={{ill|Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto|en:draft|Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto|ja|健磐龍命|simple|User:Immanuelle/Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto|fr|User:Immanuelle/Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto}}|SIS=Asotsuhime no Mikoto|SHIN=Shinhiko no Mikoto|YAYA=Yahime no Kami |}} {{Tree chart| ||||| | | |!| | | ||| ,| -|^|- |.|}} {{Tree chart| || | | | | |MOM| | | | DAD|| DAISY |MOM=Hayamikatama no Mikoto|DAD=Wakahiko no kami|DAISY=Shinhime no Mikoto}} {{Tree chart| ||||| | | |!| | | ||| !| }} {{Tree chart| |||MOM| y| DAD|| | | DAISY |MOM=Wakahime no Kami|DAD=Hikomiko no Kami|DAISY=Aso Shrine Extended Family}} {{Tree chart| ||| | ||!|}} {{Tree chart| | | | | | MOM|MOM=''Current'' Aso Shrine Priests}} {{Tree chart/end}}
==Worship== === U-no-matsuri === The Aso shrine's ''U-no-matsuri'' (卯の祭) is a 13-day event that occurs in March to welcome spring and pray for the beginning of the rice planting season. The U-no-matsuri marks the anniversary of Aso shrine's chief deity ''Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto's'' arrival in Aso. This event occurred in the second month of the lunar calendar which is March in the current calendar. The shrine's Guuji San perform sacred Shinto music and dances every day of the festival while praying for a rich harvest.<ref name="Takano-2006" />
Occurring simultaneously to the U-no-matsuri, is a prominent festival called the ''Tazukuri Matsuri'' (田作り祭り) which is celebrated over 7 days, and the ''Daihimonjiyaki'' (大火文字焼き) which is the lighting of the Chinese characters for "fire" and "flame" on the mountains which is also done around the same time and sometimes the same day as the Tazukuri Matsuri.<ref name="末吉-2018">{{Cite book|title=肥後一の宮阿蘇神社|last=末吉|first=駿一|publisher=(株）マインド|year=2018|pages=38, 39, 40 and 43}}</ref> ==See also==
